name: Limb lengthening surgery (LL)

lead: Limb lengthening is an orthopaedic procedure in which a leg bone is cut and slowly pulled apart so new bone forms in the gap, adding permanent height. It was developed for limb-length differences, deformities and conditions such as achondroplasia, and is also performed electively by people who want to be taller. In looksmaxxing forums it is the best-known route to added stature beyond genetic potential.

The process, distraction osteogenesis, was developed by Gavriil Ilizarov: after a short healing period the segments are separated gradually, new bone and soft tissue form between them, and the bone then consolidates. Clinical series describe gains of several centimetres, mostly in medical patients, and the new bone is permanent.

paras: Methods include external frames and fixators, internal nails that lengthen mechanically or magnetically, and combinations. The bone lengthens over weeks, followed by months of consolidation and physiotherapy. Forum discussion centres on cost, surgeons, countries and recovery.

Reported problems include pin-site and deep infection, bone that fails to heal, deformity, hardware failure, joint stiffness, nerve injury and further operations. China's health ministry banned the procedure in 2006 after serious side effects, according to one encyclopedia summary, and cosmetic lengthening in India has been described as high-demand and largely unregulated. It is major surgery with a long rehabilitation.

angle.text: Limb lengthening adds permanent height by cutting and slowly extending the femurs or tibias, a measurable change in stature. The technique is established in medicine for limb discrepancy and deformity and is also performed electively for cosmetic height.

lead: Limb lengthening, usually abbreviated 'LL' in looksmaxxing communities, is a surgical method that increases the length of a limb bone by cutting it and slowly separating the two ends while new bone and soft tissue form between them, a biological process called distraction osteogenesis.[1][2] For people who want to look taller it is the procedure that changes actual skeletal height: a typical elective result adds roughly 6 to 8 cm of standing height, which alters proportions, clothing fit and how tall a person appears next to others.[3][4] Orthopaedists also use it for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction, bone defects and skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia.

The modern method grew out of work by the Soviet surgeon Gavriil Ilizarov, whose circular external fixator and slow-distraction protocols made bone lengthening reliable enough for widespread use, building on earlier attempts such as Alessandro Codivilla's 1905 series, which had high rates of infection and failed healing.[1][2][5] Later techniques use internal lengthening nails, including motorised and magnetically driven ones, in place of or alongside external frames, and a procedure that once meant months wearing a metal cage has increasingly become an internal-nail operation.[1][6]

Published research is substantial for medical indications and has grown for cosmetic lengthening in otherwise healthy adults. Systematic reviews of cosmetic series report average gains in the 6 to 7 cm range, high patient-reported satisfaction, and a spectrum of complications from minor to operation-requiring.[3][4][7] Elective lengthening has also moved from orthopaedic niche to public conversation through news features, TikTok and podcasts, and on forums such as looksmax.org it is often described as the only route to stature beyond genetic potential, with the discussion centred on cost, countries and surgeons, recovery and whether the gain is worthwhile.[8][9][10][11]

paras: The surgery has three main phases: the bone is cut, a latency period of about a week allows early healing to start, and gradual distraction then separates the segments, typically about a millimetre a day delivered in a few small steps, until the target length is reached. A consolidation period follows while the regenerated bone hardens.[1] The process takes weeks to months depending on the length gained.

Patients commonly use crutches or walking aids during the lengthening and consolidation phases, and rehabilitation with physiotherapy is part of the process. Where an external frame is used, it is removed in a second operation after the bone has hardened.[2] A BuzzFeed News feature described patients walking on the day of an internal-nail operation, needing a walker for part of recovery and months of physical therapy several times a week.[10]

Gains are measured per segment. Cosmetic patients may lengthen the femurs, the tibias, or both, and published cosmetic series describe a mean gain of 6.7 cm with a range from 1.5 to 13.0 cm.[4] In the BuzzFeed feature an American surgeon said the usual ceiling with a magnetic nail is 8 cm because that is the limit of the nail.[10]

Ilizarov-type circular frames use wires and pins through the skin attached to rings and rods. Reviews describe hexapod fixators as a class of devices with six adjustable struts that allow precise multi-plane correction and are used in trauma, deformity and lengthening. A 2021 controlled clinical trial in people with achondroplasia compared a rod-based monolateral fixator against a circular multi-axial system, reporting good lengthening close to plan, a mean fixation period of around 84 days and a regenerate length of about 8.5 cm in the experimental group. Inflammation and irritation at pin sites and joint stiffness are among the described downsides of external frames.[2]

Implantable nails that lengthen from within the bone reduce external hardware. The Fitbone is described as a fully implantable motorised nail, associated in the literature with accurate correction, less scarring, lower infection risk and greater comfort.[1] A study of the Fitbone motorised nail in adolescents is among the clinical reports on this class of device.[12] Magnetically driven nails such as Precice are covered in their own entry. Registered post-market studies of Precice and Fitbone systems are currently under way.[13][14][15]

Reviews of cosmetic lengthening name three technique families: classic Ilizarov frames, lengthening over nail (LON), where a frame distracts the bone around a nail that is locked afterwards, and lengthening and then nailing (LATN), alongside fully motorised internal nails.[4][7] In the 2020 review the classic frame was the most used method (267 of 795 patients) and lengthening over nail the second (253), with implantable nails used in 63 patients, reflecting the period the studies covered.[4] A registered study of pain beliefs and function after cosmetic lengthening over nail is planned.[16]

The basic idea of gradual bone lengthening was proposed by Bernhard von Langenbeck in 1869, and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, cutting the femur and applying traction in 26 people. His results showed high rates of infection, tissue death and failed union, and the approach was not widely adopted.[1] A short report on leg-lengthening appeared in the British Medical Journal in 1951.

Gavriil Ilizarov was born in 1921 and worked in Kurgan in the Soviet Union, where he developed an external fixator in the early 1950s after observing that a cut bone, carefully separated and held stable, regrew to fill the gap. He became head of the trauma and orthopaedics department in 1955, and national attention followed in 1968 when he operated on the Olympic high jump champion Valery Brumel.[5] Over the following decades he studied the method in thousands of patients, developed the circular transfixion-wire fixator and determined suitable separation rates.[1][2]

The method reached the West after the Italian mountaineer Carlo Mauri, treated by Ilizarov in 1980 for a tibia that would not heal, publicised the result. Ilizarov lectured in Italy in 1981, an association (ASAMI) formed in 1982, and the apparatus was licensed for manufacture in 1983 before the technique arrived in North America in 1986 to 1987.[5] His 'tension-stress' principle, that gradual tension stimulates new tissue growth, was documented in canine experiments and in clinical papers published in 1989 and 1990.[17][18] Callotasis, a lengthening technique using slow distraction of callus with a dynamic axial fixator, was described in 1987 in a series of 100 bones.[19] Ilizarov died in Kurgan in 1992.[5]

From the 1990s onward intramedullary devices began to replace frames in many practices. Reviewers describe nails that can correct deformity as well as lengthen,[6] and the introduction of the Fitbone motorised nail and, from 2011, the magnetically driven Precice nail made fully internal lengthening a mainstream option.[1][20] The same technology made elective height surgery more attractive to patients who would not accept a frame, and by 2022 media features described growing interest in elective lengthening, with a 2020 BBC report cited as finding that hundreds of men have the operation each year.[10]

Medical indications include congenital limb-length discrepancy, such as congenital fibular deficiency, where lengthening is one option alongside orthoses, epiphysiodesis and amputation with prosthetic rehabilitation; a review noted that amputation for severe cases showed favourable results with fewer complications than lengthening. In achondroplasia, a systematic review found that vosoritide, growth hormone and limb lengthening all conferred benefits for height or growth, while long-term effects of growth hormone were unclear. Lengthening is also used in children with leg-length differences and in reconstruction after trauma or infection.[21][22]

Cosmetic lengthening is performed for people of otherwise typical stature. Systematic reviews of cosmetic series describe patients averaging about 25 years of age, roughly two thirds of them male, and an operation motivated by dissatisfaction with height.[7] In India it has been described as in high demand and largely unregulated, with some patients as young as 13 or 14 and reports of complications and of surgeons understating risks; China banned limb lengthening in 2006 following serious side effects.[1] A registered study plans to assess pain beliefs and function after cosmetic lengthening over nail.[16]

BuzzFeed News profiled patients and surgeons in 2022. A 25-year-old patient who was 5 feet 7 inches before surgery described paying $75,000, and a Burbank orthopaedic surgeon who performs 30 to 40 such operations a year called the surgery life-altering; a clinical psychologist interviewed said there is no standard screening process and that she focuses on patients' expectations.[10] The same article noted that patients often keep the operation private, and that a bodybuilder and podcast host who had lengthening after a leg-length problem argued it should be as accepted as other cosmetic surgery.[10]

Distraction osteogenesis reliably produces new bone in the lengthened segment, and clinical series report the planned length being achieved in most cases. A 2025 systematic review of aesthetic lower-limb lengthening covered 12 studies and 760 patients with a mean age of about 25 and found lengthening of 62 to 87 mm (average 67 mm) and patient satisfaction between 88.8 and 98 per cent.[7] The earlier 2020 review of 795 patients reported a mean follow-up of 4.9 years.[4]

Evidence specific to purely cosmetic patients is more limited than for medical indications, and published outcomes depend on the technique, surgeon and the length attempted. Lengthening of the Achilles tendon may be required alongside bone lengthening in some cases.[2] A 2025 meta-analysis of 7 studies and 489 patients compared external fixation with intramedullary nailing; it found no procedure-related deaths and lower rates of problems with nails, with external fixation satisfaction reaching 95 per cent.[23] The same review notes that a lengthening nail's length sets the typical ceiling per segment.[10]

Psychosocial outcomes are less well documented than bone outcomes. A 2024 scoping review of outcome measures in lower-limb lengthening was undertaken to inform a core outcome set, reflecting that reporting varies between studies.[24] Satisfaction figures are reported by clinical series, while the social effects people hope for, such as attention in dating or the workplace, are not systematically measured in the cosmetic literature.

A frequently cited classification separates difficulties into problems (resolved without surgery), obstacles (needing an operation to resolve) and true complications (intraoperative injuries or problems unresolved at the end of treatment).[25] In the 2020 review of cosmetic lengthening, patients averaged 0.78 problems, 0.94 obstacles and 0.15 complications each; ankle equinus was the most common problem and obstacle, and regenerate deformation and subtalar stiffness or deformity the most common complications.[4] A 2025 meta-analysis reported problems in 56 per cent of external-fixation patients and 37 per cent of nail patients.[23]

Encyclopedia summaries give approximate rates of infection (about 5 per cent), bone failing to grow in the intended direction (7 to 9 per cent), hardware failure (3 to 4.5 per cent) and improper distraction pace (about 4.5 per cent), and note that nonunion is a risk if separation is too fast.[1] Other documented issues include pin-site irritation, joint contracture, and nerve injury; experimental work found that nerves undergoing tension show changes in conduction, which is the basis of concern about stretch neuropathy.[2][26] Studies also describe soft-tissue changes in the elongating limb, and the importance of preserving blood supply and periosteum for bone formation.[17][27]

A single specialist centre in North America reported on 22 procedures referred to it for complications after nail lengthening, most performed abroad: hardware failure occurred in 23 per cent of the index operations, and malunion or nonunion in 45 per cent, mostly in the femur; the authors said all were treated successfully with no serious long-term irreversible outcomes.[28] A 2024 case report described a patient who travelled for cosmetic lengthening and had complications,[29] and a 2026 report described a rare failure of a Precice Stryde nail after cosmetic lengthening.[30] A UK paper has also discussed the burden that complications of health tourism place on the NHS.[31]

Surgeons quoted in the media attribute most complications to patients not following the rehabilitation plan, while critics argue that patients should be told that serious complications can occur even when they do.[10][1] Elective lengthening in healthy people raises an ethical question that orthopaedists debate: a 2025 survey of 496 US adults found 63 per cent considered it ethically acceptable and 70 per cent considered it equivalent to other cosmetic surgery, while 7 per cent would consider it themselves.[32]

China's health ministry banned limb lengthening in 2006 following serious side effects, according to encyclopedia summaries, while cosmetic lengthening in India has been described as high-demand and largely unregulated.[1] Magnetic nails are cleared by the US FDA as devices for lengthening indications, with the first Precice system cleared in 2011, and one encyclopedia-style summary notes a temporary suspension of the EU certificate for Precice in 2021.[20]

Cosmetic lengthening is generally not covered by insurance, and published cost reports vary with country and technique. One looksmax.org post lists external-fixator prices from about $6 to 10 thousand and internal-nail methods at roughly $12 to 25 thousand in India,[8] while a patient in the BuzzFeed feature said his operation cost $75,000.[10] Forum threads on financing the surgery are common.[33]

Published clinical work consists largely of case series, retrospective studies and a few controlled trials, mostly in medical rather than cosmetic patients. Examples include a controlled trial of a monolateral rod fixator versus a circular system in achondroplasia (14 patients, 28 segments), a randomised trial of kinesiology taping to reduce lower-limb oedema during Ilizarov treatment, a randomised trial of hydroxyapatite-coated pins and pin-track infection in leg lengthening for short stature,[34] and a retrospective study of limb lengthening with three-dimensional deformity correction. Landmark papers on Ilizarov's method and its complications are among the most cited in the field.[25][18]

For cosmetic lengthening specifically, a 2020 systematic review in Bone and Joint Research (11 studies, 795 patients),[4] a 2025 systematic review of aesthetic techniques (12 studies, 760 patients)[7] and a 2025 meta-analysis (7 studies, 489 patients)[23] summarise outcomes; the original studies are mostly retrospective. Surveys of the public and of surgeons add attitude data,[32][35] and a content analysis of the 50 most-viewed English-language TikTok videos on height surgery (186.5 million views) found 60 per cent medically accurate, including 80 per cent of those made by health-care professionals.[36]

Registered studies include post-market evaluations of Precice nails in children and adults, a Fitbone patient-reported pain and quality-of-life study, a Google Trends analysis of public interest in limb lengthening, and a planned study of pain beliefs after cosmetic lengthening over nail.[13][15][16][37][38]

On looksmax.org and similar forums, LL is described as the only route to permanently increase height, and threads compare surgeons, countries and device types. One widely read post says external fixator procedures in India start around $6 to 10 thousand and internal nail methods run roughly $12 to 25 thousand, names surgeons and hospitals, and notes trade-offs: external methods mean more pain and scarring, internal methods cost more, and months of follow-up are needed.[8] Other users describe the surgery as costly and painful, and some weigh whether the money would be better spent on other procedures or purchases.[9]

Thread titles show the range of the conversation: debate over whether leg lengthening is the surgery that most increases dating 'SMV', whether it is the only surgery most members should consider, how to afford it, what the risks are, and whether a one-to-two-inch gain is realistic.[33][39][40][41] Others discuss the interaction between lengthening and later muscle development.[42]

A 2025 qualitative study in Sociology of Health and Illness analysed 8,072 comments on a looksmaxxing board with about 6 million monthly visitors. The authors, Michael Halpin and colleagues, reported that the community pushes men toward major bodily changes such as leg-lengthening surgery and mewing, and concluded that such communities can harm participants' health.[43] Reporting in the technology press has also tracked public interest: Hacker News threads on lengthening drew hundreds of comments in 2022.[11]

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing communities LL is treated as the definitive but costly height intervention, with discussion about where to have it done, which technique to choose and whether it is worth the recovery.[8][9]
